documents: Mark et al. (2022), Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2021GL096863, published version corrected 23 AUG 2022, with erratum (PDF, 10 pages)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (n of 10), which coincide with PDF pages counted from 1; supplementary material not supplied

entry.evidence: but the full extent of the slab window remains poorly defined

sequences.source_document: Mark et al. 2022, GRL, corrected version of record (PDF)

steps.action: The authors take from earlier GIA and geodetic studies the hypothesis that low-viscosity slab-window mantle beneath the icefields speeds the GIA response and drives extreme uplift.
steps.quote: Low-viscosity mantle in the slab window beneath the icefields is expected to speed the GIA response

steps.action: They pose the question of the full extent of the slab window and of lateral viscosity variation beneath the icefields, which kinematic reconstructions and local tomography leave poorly constrained.
steps.quote: but the full extent of the slab window remains poorly defined

steps.action: They assemble broadband records from the new GUANACO deployment plus SEPA, CRSP, permanent networks and ENAP stations.
steps.quote: we use seismic data recently collected by the GUANACO broadband seismic deployment

steps.action: They derive Rayleigh-wave phase and group velocity maps from ambient-noise tomography (8-40 s) and Helmholtz earthquake tomography (20-100 s). They merge these into 8-100 s dispersion curves, with QC relaxed for CRSP stations.
steps.quote: Phase velocity dispersion curves from 8 to 100 s were constructed by combining the results from ambient noise and earthquake tomography

steps.action: They compute P receiver functions by multitaper deconvolution and form composite station RFs by harmonic decomposition.
steps.quote: P-to-s RFs were then calculated using the multitaper deconvolution method

steps.action: They jointly invert dispersion curves and RFs for 1D Vsv-depth models with a 14-parameter Bayesian MCMC, using priors from H-k stacking and K-means sediment clustering plus physical velocity constraints.
steps.quote: We inverted for 1D velocity-depth models using a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method

steps.action: They check the K-means 'thick sediment' prior classification against the mapped extent of the Austral-Magallanes Basin.
steps.quote: The “thick” sediment cluster agreed well with the mapped extent of the Austral-Magallanes Basin

steps.action: Where station inversions failed to fit, notably in the thick-sediment basin, they adjust the layer-thickness priors. They then invert dispersion alone on a 0.3° grid and combine and smooth grid and station results into the 3D model.
steps.quote: Prior distributions for the sediment and crustal layer thicknesses were then adjusted in places where the inversion failed to find a well-fitted model.

steps.action: They convert velocity anomalies relative to STW105 into temperature and then viscosity anomalies, using dry olivine diffusion creep, the IJ05-R2 reference viscosity and a temperature fraction fixed at 0.65.
steps.quote: The seismic anomalies were used to estimate temperature anomalies relative to a global average temperature model

steps.action: They report low mantle velocities throughout the slab window (minimum <4.1 km/s at 50 km, ~8% slow), most intense north of 49°S, with uncertainties of ~0.1 km/s.
steps.quote: Mantle velocities are low throughout the inferred slab window region, with a minimum velocity less than 4.1 km/s

steps.action: They check the mapped anomaly against independent references: the western edge against kinematic slab-window reconstructions and the adakite trend, and the fast southeastern block against xenolith evidence of thicker lithosphere.
steps.quote: the western edge of the anomaly at 100 km depth aligns with estimates of the extent of the subducting Antarctic slab

steps.action: From sub-Moho velocities (4.1 vs 4.5 km/s in STW105) and cross sections, they infer that the lithospheric mantle is absent near the CTJ.
steps.quote: indicating that the lithospheric mantle is missing in the youngest part of the slab window

steps.action: They propose that slab-window mantle dynamics thermally eroded the base of the overriding plate.
steps.quote: The absence of lithospheric mantle near the CTJ suggests that mantle dynamics associated with the slab window have eroded the base of the plate.

steps.action: They cite thermo-mechanical ridge-subduction models that predict thermal erosion of the overriding plate.
steps.quote: [...] the overriding plate is predicted by thermo-mechanical models of ridge subduction

steps.action: They set the inferred thinning beside earlier inferences from heat flow, crustal thickness and GIA model fits, and beside similar Antarctic Peninsula interpretations.
steps.quote: Previous studies have inferred that the Patagonian lithosphere has thinned above the slab window

steps.action: They refine the mechanism: erosion likely needs melt or fluids from decompression of upwelling asthenosphere, possibly aided by vigorous mantle flow seen in shear-wave splitting.
steps.quote: The process of thermal erosion likely requires the presence of melt or fluids

steps.action: For the intact southern lithosphere they state two rivals, pre-existing thicker lithosphere or less efficient early erosion, without choosing between them.
steps.quote: it is possible that the lithosphere in the south was thicker prior to the opening of the slab window

steps.action: They exclude re-formation of mantle lithosphere by conductive cooling on timescale grounds, given ridge-segment entry ages of 18-3 Ma.
steps.quote: timescales of conductive cooling are too short relative to the age of the slab window

steps.action: For the >10 km north-south crustal thinning they reject surface erosion as the sole cause and note that a Mendocino-type mechanism conflicts with relief data. They leave other proposed causes open.
steps.quote: is unlikely to be entirely due to surface erosion since the thinning is not primarily in the upper crust

steps.action: They take from published GIA models two rival explanations of the uplift: lower viscosity beneath the NPI than the SPI, or more NPI ice loss than estimated.
steps.quote: reproducing observed uplift rates requires either mantle viscosities that are significantly lower beneath the NPI compared to the SPI or more ice mass loss

steps.action: They compare the location of the slowest anomaly and the estimated viscosity map with the two rivals and find them consistent with lower viscosity beneath the NPI.
steps.quote: north of 49°S is consistent with the former explanation

steps.action: Their viscosities are mostly higher than geodetic estimates. They attribute the mismatch to uncertain auxiliaries such as the temperature fraction and keep the relative pattern.
steps.quote: absolute viscosity values we obtain are highly sensitive to uncertain parameters such as the fraction of velocity variation due to temperature

steps.action: They derive expectations from the model: a three-dimensional GIA response, shorter-wavelength signals over thin lithosphere, and dominantly eastward horizontal motion east of the SPI.
steps.quote: the geodetic response to glacial unloading in Patagonia will be highly three-dimensional

steps.action: They compare the eastward-motion prediction with published GNSS horizontal displacements along the eastern northern SPI.
steps.quote: GNSS observations of horizontal surface displacements support this prediction

steps.action: They keep the claim that slab-window structure (slow mantle, eroded lithosphere) implies heterogeneous low viscosity, and that GIA models of the region must include it.
steps.quote: Lateral heterogeneity in mantle viscosity and lithospheric thickness, guided by seismic models and other geophysical observations, must be incorporated into GIA modeling in this region.

steps.action: Per the erratum, a bug in the public ASWMS software was found. The affected calculations were redone and the corrected model was reported to support all conclusions.
steps.quote: All of the affected calculations have been redone; the results were not significantly affected

tree.answer: Yes: slab window and rapid uplift already documented
No: mantle velocity, lithosphere thickness and viscosity inferred by inversion
Map full slab-window extent and lithospheric structure; constrain viscosity for GIA
Partly: cited GIA rivals (viscosity vs ice loss); southern lithosphere rivals
Partly: anomaly location separates GIA rivals; southern rivals not separated
Found: natural slab window, passive seismic data
Partly: product checked against kinematics, adakites, xenoliths; rerun after bug; temperature fraction not varied
Kept: slow, eroded slab-window mantle; low viscosity beneath NPI

end.claim: A slow uppermost-mantle anomaly (<4.1 km/s, uncertainty ~0.1 km/s) spans the Patagonian slab window, is strongest north of 49°S, and shows thermally eroded lithospheric mantle near the CTJ, implying lower viscosity beneath the NPI and northern SPI.

decisive_move.sentence: The Bayesian MCMC joint inversion of Rayleigh dispersion and receiver functions across the new GUANACO array produced the velocity model on which every claim rests.

gates.evidence: The GUANACO deployment belongs to a project on the solid Earth response to post-Little Ice Age retreat (Magnani et al. 2020, p. 2). That suggests the GIA/slab-window hypothesis motivated acquisition, but the paper does not state this (inference). The GIA rivals (low NPI viscosity vs more ice loss, p. 6) could have been contradicted by the location of the slowest anomaly. The velocity model itself faces only consistency checks against kinematic reconstructions, adakites and xenoliths (p. 4). No analysis or threshold is said to be fixed in advance; the temperature fraction 0.65 is adopted from Wu et al. 2013 (p. 4).

imports.item: K-means clustering (scikit-learn) to classify stations by sediment thickness
Markov chain Monte Carlo Bayesian inversion

novelty_claims.quote: Here, we present the first regional seismic velocity model covering the entire north-south extent of the slab window.

limits:
No peer-review file was supplied. Reviewers R. M. Russo and V. Klemann are thanked (p. 8), but what they asked for cannot be coded, so there is no review sequence. Supplementary figures (S1-S8, uncertainty maps, posteriors) are cited but not supplied.

The velocity model is estimate_with_resolution. Sub-claims carry other statuses:
- Thermal erosion of the lithospheric mantle near the CTJ: best_explanation; no rival to erosion is tested.
- The link between low NPI viscosity and rapid uplift: best_explanation among two cited rivals.
- Absolute viscosity values: estimate without stated uncertainty, sensitive to the temperature fraction.
- Crustal-thinning cause: no_conclusion.
- Cause of intact southern lithosphere: no_conclusion between two rivals.

On robustness:
- The temperature fraction (0.65) is not varied. The claim that the pattern is unchanged is asserted, not shown.
- The wet-creep insensitivity is stated with a citation, not demonstrated (coded as not performed here).
- The erratum reports recalculation after a software bug without showing the differences.

Composition is none_fits: this is a problem-driven imaging and estimation study. It has no crucial test and no repeated independent traces, and the new array data serve a question already posed, so it is not capability_first.

Whether the GIA hypothesis directed the array deployment is inference from the cited project abstract title.

disagreements.target: Previous geodetic viscosity estimates (Lange et al., 2014; Richter et al., 2016)
disagreements.support: Seismically derived viscosities are mostly higher than the geodetic values, which the authors attribute to uncertain conversion parameters while keeping the low-viscosity pattern.
disagreements.quote: Our estimated viscosities are mostly higher than the values obtained by previous geodetic studies

disagreements.target: GIA models assuming a radially layered mantle
disagreements.support: Strong lateral viscosity heterogeneity in the velocity model implies a three-dimensional response that 1D models cannot capture, especially horizontal motions.
disagreements.quote: cannot be fully described by symmetric deformation predicted for a radially [...]

disagreements.target: GIA explanation requiring more NPI ice mass loss than previously estimated (Lange et al., 2014; Russo et al., 2022)
disagreements.support: The slowest velocity anomaly lies north of 49°S, favouring the rival explanation of lower viscosity beneath the NPI.
disagreements.quote: north of 49°S is consistent with the former explanation

alternatives_considered.reason: to obtain adequate data coverage near the CTJ

alternatives_considered.chosen: Composite RF from zeroth-order harmonic decomposition
alternatives_considered.reason: average used when azimuthal coverage was insufficient to fit harmonics

alternatives_considered.chosen: Temperature fraction of velocity anomaly = 0.65 (Wu et al., 2013)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: A different fraction appropriate to Patagonia
alternatives_considered.reason: value found in a geodetic study of North America and Fennoscandia; variation would not change the relative pattern

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Southern lithosphere thicker before slab window opened; thermal erosion less efficient in early stages

alternatives_considered.chosen: None chosen (surface erosion as sole cause rejected)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Surface erosion; Mendocino-type ephemeral thickening then thinning; preexisting structure; terrane overthrusting; thermal erosion; tectonic extension
alternatives_considered.reason: thinning not primarily in upper crust; relief trend does not match flexural predictions; further measurements needed

alternatives_considered.reason: slowest velocity anomaly lies north of 49°S
